title: Keeping data and secrets out
objectives: Write a `.gitignore` for data, outputs, the virtual environment and keys, and check it works
Keep an API key in an environment variable, `.env` or a dotfile
Say why a committed secret must be revoked

screens.prose: Your Stage 1 project folder is ready for GitHub. Before the first commit, decide what goes in. Anything committed is copied to every clone, forever.
screens.question: Sort each file: commit it, or keep it out of Git.

hints.text: Could the file be rebuilt from the others? Is it private?
These are made by your code or by a command.
Commit what you wrote. Keep out what code rebuilds (data, results, the virtual environment) and the key.

feedback.correct: Commit what you wrote; keep out what can be rebuilt, and the key.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each file: did I write it, or can it be made again?

byKey.t-data: You committed the data. download.py fetches it again, and 41 MB would sit in every clone forever.
byKey.t-res: You committed an output. plot.py makes it again on every run, so each run would show up as a change.
byKey.t-venv: You committed the virtual environment. It is 312 MB and only works on your machine; requirements.txt rebuilds it.
byKey.t-env: You committed the key. Anyone with the repository could use it, and it stays in the history.
byKey.t-req: requirements.txt is how others rebuild your environment. It must be committed.
byKey.t-test: The test is code you wrote, and readers run it. Commit it.
byKey.t-readme: The README is the page GitHub shows. Commit it.
byKey.t-py: returns.py is the project itself. Commit it.

explain.text: You committed the four files you wrote. The data, the results and `.venv/` can all be rebuilt from them. The key is private, so it must never be committed at all.

screens.prose:
As in l3, you list the files to keep out in `.gitignore`, one pattern per line. A name ending in `/` means a folder. Git then leaves matching files untracked and stops listing them.

```sh
# .gitignore
data/
results/
.venv/
.env
```

state.caption: `git status` listed these before you made .gitignore

screens.question: You run `git status` again. Tap the entries it still lists.

hints.text: Which entries match a line of .gitignore?
Nothing in .gitignore matches this file's own name.
data/, results/, .venv/ and .env match. Everything else is still listed, the new .gitignore included.

feedback.correct: Your four files, plus .gitignore itself, which you commit too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only entries matching a pattern disappear.

byKey.no-gitignore: You left out .gitignore itself. It is a new file, and it should be committed so every clone ignores the same things.
byKey.r0c0: .env matches the last pattern, so it is no longer listed.

explain.text: The four patterns hid data/, results/, .venv/ and .env. The five entries left are what you commit. That includes `.gitignore` itself, so every clone ignores the same files.

screens.prose:
A colleague's `.gitignore` starts with `*.csv` instead of `data/`. Her test reads a 10-row file, `tests/prices_small.csv`. On a fresh clone the test fails. She asks Git why:

```sh
$ git check-ignore -v tests/prices_small.csv
.gitignore:1:*.csv    tests/prices_small.csv
```
screens.question: What does the output tell her?

options.text: Line 1, `*.csv`, ignores the test's file, so it was never committed
The file is committed and safe
options.why: You read the output as a success. check-ignore prints only for paths that a pattern ignores.
The line is valid. It does exactly what it says, which is too much.

options.text: Git refuses to run the tests
options.why: Git never runs tests. The test fails because its data file is missing from the clone.

hints.text: check-ignore prints a path only when it is ignored. What does each part name?
This is the line that matched.
The output names the file, line 1 and the pattern `*.csv`. That pattern caught the test data too.

feedback.correct: Line 1 caught a file the test needs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the output as: file, line, pattern, path.

byKey.safe: You read the output as a success. It names the rule that ignores the file.

explain.text: `*.csv` matches every .csv in every folder, test data included, so it never reached GitHub. Replace it with `data/`, which matches only the downloads. Run `git check-ignore -v` on any file you are unsure of.

screens.prose:
Last week you committed `data/spy.csv` by mistake. Today you add `data/` to `.gitignore` and download fresh prices for SPY and QQQ. `git status` shows:

```sh
modified:   data/spy.csv
```
screens.question: Why is spy.csv listed, but not qqq.csv?

options.text: `.gitignore` only affects files Git is not tracking yet
`.gitignore` works only after it is committed
options.why: qqq.csv is already hidden, so the pattern works now. The difference is that spy.csv was committed.
`data/` matches both files; qqq.csv proves it. The pattern is fine.

options.text: spy.csv is too big to ignore
options.why: Git ignores files of any size. Size has nothing to do with it.

hints.text: What differs between the two rows?
This column differs.
spy.csv was committed before the pattern existed. Git keeps tracking a file it already tracks.

feedback.correct: Ignore rules only apply to untracked files.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what is different about the two files.

byKey.commit: You expected the rule to need a commit. It already hides qqq.csv, so it works; spy.csv is different because it was committed.

explain.text: Git keeps tracking any file it already tracks, whatever `.gitignore` says. Run `git rm --cached data/spy.csv` and commit: Git stops tracking it, and your copy stays on disk. Last week's commit still holds the old prices in the history.

screens.prose:
Keys belong outside the code, in an **environment variable**: a named value the shell hands to every program it starts. `key.py` prints one:

```python
import os
print(os.environ.get("POLYGON_API_KEY"))
```
screens.question: What does the last row print?

options.why: You expected `export` to last. It sets the variable for that window only, and window 2 never ran it.
`.get` returns None for a missing name. Square brackets would raise the KeyError.
A missing variable is not an empty one. `.get` gives None, and print shows the word None.

hints.text: Did window 2 ever run `export`?
This row ran in a different shell.
Each terminal is its own shell. window 2 has no such variable, so `.get` returns None.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. An exported variable lives only in the shell that set it.

byKey.key: You expected `export` to stick. It lasts until that window closes, and only there.

explain.text: `export` set the key in window 1 and the programs it starts. Window 2 is a separate shell that never ran it. Next we make the shell set it every time.

screens.prose: Files whose names start with a dot are **dotfiles**. `~/.zshrc` sits in your home folder, outside every project. The shell runs it each time a terminal opens. You add two lines, save, and in the same window type `bt SPY`. An **alias** is a short name for a longer command.
screens.question: What happens?

options.why: You expected the shell to notice the edit. It read .zshrc when the window opened, before your new lines existed.
An alias runs its command; it does not print it. Here it is not defined yet anyway.
~/.zshrc is in your home folder, outside the project. Git never sees it.

hints.text: When does the shell read ~/.zshrc?
Only when a terminal opens. This window opened before your edit.

feedback.correct: This window read .zshrc before you changed it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when the shell reads the file.

byKey.runs: You expected the edit to apply at once. Run `source ~/.zshrc` or open a new window first.

explain.text: The shell read `~/.zshrc` when this window opened, so `bt` is unknown here. `source ~/.zshrc` reads it again now; new windows read it anyway. The key lives in your home folder, so no `git add` can pick it up.

screens.prose: In commit C you pasted your live key into `config.py` to test a download, then pushed. In D you deleted that line and pushed again. The repository is public.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: C added the key; D removed it. Both are on GitHub.

screens.question: Is the key safe now?

options.text: No: C still holds it. Revoke the key and make a new one
Yes: the latest files have no key
options.why: You looked only at the newest files. Every commit stays readable, and C has the key.
Ignoring a file changes nothing already committed. C keeps its copy.
Revert adds a new commit that undoes C. C itself stays in the history, key and all.

hints.text: What does a commit hold, and can it change later?
This commit was pushed with the key in it.
C is a snapshot with the key, and it is on GitHub. Anyone can run `git show C:config.py`. Treat the key as stolen.

feedback.correct: A pushed secret is a leaked secret. Revoke it first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Deleting the line made a new commit; it did not change C.

byKey.latest: You checked the latest files only. C is still in every clone, and bots scan public history for keys within minutes.
byKey.revert: Revert makes a new commit; it never removes one. C still holds the key.

explain.text: D removed the key from the latest files, but C still holds it on GitHub and in every clone. The only safe fix is to revoke the key at the provider and issue a new one. Rewriting history can tidy up afterwards, but copies may already exist.

screens.prose:
Here is the pattern you built. Keep comments on their own lines in `.gitignore`: a `#` after a pattern becomes part of it.

```sh
# .gitignore for a quant project
# prices that download.py fetches
data/
# outputs the code makes again
results/
# the virtual environment
.venv/
# API keys
.env
__pycache__/
```

The key goes in `.env` or `~/.zshrc`, and code reads it from the environment.
screens.question: How do you check that `.env` is really ignored?

options.why: That shows the rules, not whether one matches. A typo would go unnoticed.
The log shows commits. An ignored file never appears there, but neither does one you have not committed yet.

hints.text: Which command answered the question about the test data?
`git check-ignore -v` names the matching line, or prints nothing.

feedback.correct: It prints the line that ignores .env, or nothing if none does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You want a command that tests one path against the rules.

explain.text: check-ignore tests a path against every pattern and names the one that matches. No output means the file is not ignored. Run it before the first `git add .`.

screens.prose: Your downloader fetches ten years of daily bars for SPY, QQQ, IWM, EFA and TLT. It needs your live key. `.env` holds `POLYGON_API_KEY=pk_live_...` and is listed in `.gitignore`. `load_dotenv()`, from the python-dotenv package, copies `.env` into the environment.
screens.question: After `load_dotenv()`, which line should `download.py` use to get the key?

options.why: You gave the live key as a fallback. That writes it into download.py, which is committed.
You wrote the key into the code. download.py is committed, so the key would be on GitHub.
No leak, but the path exists only on your laptop. A reviewer or a clone cannot run it.

hints.text: Which file is committed, and which is not?
This file goes to GitHub.
The key must appear only in .env. download.py should name the variable and nothing more.

feedback.correct: The code names the variable; the value stays in the ignored `.env`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The key must not appear in any committed file.

byKey.default: You put the key in as a default. A fallback is still text in a committed file.

explain.text: `os.environ[...]` names the key without containing it. If `.env` is missing it fails loudly with a KeyError, which is what you want. Commit a `.env.example` holding `POLYGON_API_KEY=` with no value, so others know what to set.

ideas: Commit what you wrote. Ignore what can be rebuilt (data, outputs, `.venv/`) and every secret.
`.gitignore` only affects untracked files. Check a path with `git check-ignore -v`.
Code reads keys from the environment. The value lives in an ignored `.env` or in `~/.zshrc`.

formula.name: Reading a key
formula.note: The code names the key; the value never enters a committed file.

summary.trap: Deleting a pushed key in a new commit does not remove it. The old commit still holds it: revoke the key.

quiz.prose: You committed `results/equity.png` and now want Git to stop tracking it. You run `git rm --cached results/equity.png` and commit.
quiz.question: What happens to the file on your laptop?

options.text: It stays on disk; Git stops tracking it
It is deleted from your folder
options.why: `--cached` removes it from Git only. Without it, `git rm` would delete the file too.

options.text: It vanishes from every old commit
options.why: Old commits never change. They still hold the image.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the option: cached means the staging area, not your folder.

explain.text: `git rm --cached` takes the file out of the next commit and leaves your copy. Add `results/` to .gitignore so it stays untracked. Older commits still include it.

quiz.prose: Your project needs `POLYGON_API_KEY`. A new colleague clones it and has no idea what to set.
quiz.question: What do you commit to tell them?

options.why: That commits your key. Anyone with the repository could use it.
A README is committed and public. The key would leak at once.

options.text: Nothing: they will see the error
options.why: They will, but a KeyError does not say where to get a key. A template does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share which variable to set, not its value.

explain.text: `.env.example` lists the variables with empty values. The colleague copies it to `.env` and fills in their own key. The pattern `.env` ignores only the exact name, so the example is committed.

quiz.prose: You find your live API key in a commit pushed to a public repository three days ago.
quiz.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Revoke the key at the provider and issue a new one

options.why: That hides it from the latest files only. The old commit still holds it.
It was public for three days. Clones and scanners may already have it.

options.text: Rewrite the history to remove it
options.why: Worth doing later, but copies made in three days stay out of your reach. The key itself must die.

feedback.correct: A leaked key is spent. Revoke it before anything else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which step makes the leaked key useless.

explain.text: Only revoking the key stops someone who already copied it. Then move it to `.env`, and clean the history if you wish. Order matters: revoke first.

quiz.prose: `.gitignore` holds one line: `.env`. The project has `.env`, `.env.example` and `config/.env`.
quiz.question: Which of them are ignored?

options.why: A pattern with no slash matches that name in any folder, so config/.env is caught too.
`.env.example` is a different name. The pattern matches the exact name `.env` only.
The pattern has no star, so `.env.example` does not match. config/.env does.

feedback.correct: The exact name, in any folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A pattern with no slash matches the exact name anywhere.

explain.text: `.env` matches files named exactly `.env`, at any depth. `.env.example` has a longer name, so it is not matched. That is why the example file can be committed.
